title: Decidability of equivalence for unambiguous context-free grammars
formal: Is it decidable, given two finite context-free grammars \(G_1,G_2\) over the same finite terminal alphabet and promised that both are unambiguous, whether \(L(G_1)=L(G_2)\)?
why: This basic equivalence problem tests the algorithmic power of unique parsing beyond deterministic context-free language descriptions.

importance.reason: A longstanding decidability boundary for language equivalence under the fundamental unique-parse restriction.

sentences: An unambiguous context-free grammar has at most one parse tree for every generated word.
Two such grammars are given with the promise of unambiguity.
The task is to decide whether they generate exactly the same finite words.
No deterministic-pushdown or regular-language restriction is imposed.
The question asks for a terminating decision procedure without any prescribed complexity bound.

definitions: A context-free grammar \(G=(V,\Sigma,P,S)\) has finite disjoint sets of nonterminals \(V\) and terminals \(\Sigma\), a start symbol \(S\in V\), and a finite set of productions \(A\to u\), with \(A\in V\) and \(u\in(V\cup\Sigma)^*\). Empty right-hand sides and unit productions are allowed. A parse tree is a finite ordered rooted tree with root \(S\) whose nonterminal nodes expand by productions; its terminal leaves read from left to right form the generated word, possibly empty. The language \(L(G)\subseteq\Sigma^*\) consists of words with such a tree. Unambiguous means at most one parse tree for each word, not at most one order of expanding a fixed tree. Both grammars, alphabet lists and full production strings are explicit finite inputs with binary symbol identifiers and delimiters; duplicate written productions are identified. The decision algorithm is one deterministic Turing machine that terminates on every syntactically valid pair and is correct whenever both grammars satisfy the promise. On pairs violating the promise it may return either answer. Invalid syntax may be rejected. It receives no proof of unambiguity and need not decide that promise. There is no running-time bound, determinism promise for the grammars or restriction to regular or unary languages.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof that such a decision machine exists, or a Lean proof that the promised equivalence problem is undecidable. A result for deterministic pushdown presentations, comparison with only a finite automaton, or a semidecision procedure for inequivalence does not settle the complete two-grammar question.

context_blocks.text: Each generated word has a unique parse in an unambiguous grammar, but the grammar need not make deterministic parsing choices. The question compares two languages under that promise.
The author’s problem list separates this question from the stronger problem of comparing arbitrary derivation multiplicities.

notes: Read the author’s exact promised equivalence question, distinguishing it from arbitrary CFG equivalence, deterministic-language equivalence and bag equivalence.
Defined finite parse trees including epsilon and unit rules, explicit grammar inputs, total decision behavior and correctness only under the unambiguity promise.
Preserved decidability rather than imposing a complexity endpoint, and supplied problem-specific context, significance and Lean certification.
